name: SMB Server Status (smbstatus)
description: Shows active Samba connections, open files, and locked files on the local Samba server — confirms which shares are in use and by whom.

examples.label: Show shares, connections, and open files

notes: Server-side command; requires being logged onto the Samba host. Useful during a post-access review to see who else is connected and what shares are mounted. Output includes PID, user, group, machine, and protocol version per session.

recommended.note: Enumerate the same shares from the network perspective
Review Samba config for dangerous share settings

defense.why_it_works:
smbstatus output in the Footprinting module shows 'Signing: False' on active SMB sessions. When SMB signing is disabled or not required, attackers can perform relay attacks against sessions observed on the network.

[MITRE T1049] Adversaries enumerate network connections to/from compromised systems using netstat, ss, lsof, PowerShell Get-NetTCPConnection, or WMI/API calls — revealing connected systems, services, and network topology to plan next steps.
defense.prerequisites: Local/administrative access on the Samba server to run smbstatus (or equivalent visibility into active sessions).
defense.impact: Visibility into active SMB sessions and, critically, whether signing is disabled — identifying viable NTLM-relay targets.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1049 AN0903] Detect usage of commands or binaries (netstat, PowerShell Get-NetTCPConnection) and WMI/API calls to enumerate local or remote network connections. [AN0904] Use of netstat, ss, lsof, or custom shell scripts to list current network connections — often paired with privilege escalation or staging activities.
defense.artifacts: Local command execution on the SMB server; no network footprint against a remote target.
defense.prevention: Enable and require SMB signing server-wide: set 'smb2 security mode = required' in smb.conf (Samba/Linux) or via Group Policy on Windows (Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)).
defense.misconfiguration: SMB null sessions are allowed — the server accepts anonymous (unauthenticated) IPC$ connections, exposing share lists, user lists, password policy, and domain information. On older Windows versions (pre-2008 R2) this was the default. On modern systems it can be re-enabled by misconfiguration or GPO rollback. Additionally, SMB signing may be disabled, enabling relay attacks.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Windows Registry — null sessions enabled:
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters
#   RestrictAnonymous = 0      <-- allows null session enumeration
#   RestrictAnonymousSAM = 0   <-- exposes SAM account list anonymously

# SMB signing disabled (relay attack enabler):
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters
#   RequireSecuritySignature = 0
#   EnableSecuritySignature  = 0

# Verify current state:
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMBQUIC,RequireSecuritySignature
defense.secure_config:
# Disable null sessions:
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' \
    -Name RestrictAnonymous -Value 2
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' \
    -Name RestrictAnonymous -Value 1

# Enable SMB signing (blocks NTLM relay attacks):
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force
Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force

# GPO path:
# Computer Config > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options:
#   'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled
#   'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts' = Enabled
#   'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' = Enabled
